The Brownian case has only one factor of \Delta t_i per term, so the sum telescopes to t directly, with no extra \Delta t_i left for the mesh inequality to absorb. Differentiability buys you that one extra power of \Delta t_i, and that one extra power is what makes the sum vanish.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
section: 1.6 Geometric interpretation of why [W]_t = t makes Brownian motion non-differentiable
text:
1.6 Geometric interpretation of why [W]_t = t makes Brownian motion non-differentiable
The quadratic-variation results of the previous sections have a vivid geometric reading. A function’s local smoothness is what a magnifying glass reveals: zoom far enough into a differentiable curve and it looks like a straight line — its tangent — whereas zoom into a Brownian path and it stays as irregular as ever. The two subsections below make this contrast precise, and it is the same contrast that decides whether a squared increment survives in the limit.

1.6.1 Smooth functions
A differentiable function has a well-defined slope at every point. Geometrically that means it is locally linear: over a small step \Delta t its increment is f'(t)\,\Delta t = O(\Delta t), proportional to the step. Take even a high-curvature region and zoom in, and the curve bends less and less, settling toward its tangent line (Figure 4). The departure from the tangent over a window of width \Delta t is the curvature term \tfrac{1}{2} f''\,(\Delta t)^2 = O(\Delta t^2) — it shrinks faster than the window, so the squared increment is negligible next to \Delta t, which is why a smooth path has zero quadratic variation (Section 1.4).








Figure 4: Left: a parabola with its horizontal tangent at the minimum (dashed), the dotted box marking the minimum region. Right: that boxed region magnified, at the same axis scale — the curve is far shallower and lies close to the tangent, with only a slight residual bend.





The magnified curve is shallower but not perfectly straight — a slight bend remains at finite zoom, and zooming further would reduce it further still, approaching a straight line in the limit. Because the bend shrinks this way, the squared increment is negligible: (\Delta f)^2 = O(\Delta t^2) \to 0 relative to \Delta t. This is the geometric face of the zero quadratic variation derived in Section 1.4. Brownian motion, we will now see, refuses to straighten.


1.6.2 Brownian motion
The quadratic-variation result [W]_t = t (Equation 2) is the algebraic statement that a Brownian increment scales as \Delta W \sim \sqrt{\Delta t}. That square-root scaling has an immediate geometric consequence: the slope of a chord over a step is \Delta W / \Delta t \sim 1/\sqrt{\Delta t} \to \infty as \Delta t \to 0, so the difference quotient blows up rather than converging to a finite slope, and the path is not continuously differentiable. In fact a classical theorem [5] establishes the stronger property that Brownian paths are almost surely nowhere differentiable; the scaling here is the intuition behind that result, not a proof of it. Figure 5 makes this visible through statistical self-similarity [6]: zooming into any sub-interval and rescaling by the same \sqrt{\Delta t} law reproduces a path just as irregular as the original, so there is no scale at which the path ever straightens out.








Figure 5: Left: a Brownian sample path on [0, 1], with a small sub-interval [a, b] boxed. Right: that boxed sub-interval, rescaled by \times 20 in time and \times\sqrt{20} in value — the zoom is just as irregular as the whole path, with no smoother, straighter segment revealed.





The same \sqrt{\Delta t} scaling is what makes a squared increment matter. A smooth curve flattens toward its tangent under magnification, so its increment is O(\Delta t) and its square O(\Delta t^2) — negligible. The Brownian path never flattens: its increment is O(\sqrt{\Delta t}), so its square is O(\Delta t), the same order as dt itself. That is the content of [W]_t = t, and it is why a squared Brownian increment cannot be discarded — the fact we turn into a precise calculus rule in the next section.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
1.7 The (dW)^2 = dt rule
What Equation 2 says at the level of infinitesimals is that (\Delta W)^2 behaves, in sum, like \Delta t. This is the meaning of the working rule

\boxed{(dW)^2 = dt}
\tag{3}
— not a literal pointwise equality of random variables, but a calculus rule for what sums of (\Delta W)^2 terms converge to inside an integral.

1.7.1 What the rule means inside an integral
The precise content of Equation 3 is an integral statement. For any sufficiently regular deterministic function f on [0, t],

\boxed{\int_0^t f(s)\,(dW_s)^2 \;:=\; \lim_{\|\Pi\| \to 0} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2 \;=\; \int_0^t f(s)\, ds}
\tag{4}
with convergence in L^2 — the same calculation that gave [W]_t = t, now carrying the weight f.
Mean: By linearity of expectation,

\mathbb{E}\!\Big[\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big] \;=\; \sum_i f(t_i)\, \mathbb{E}\big[(\Delta W_i)^2\big]

Substituting \mathbb{E}\big[(\Delta W_i)^2\big] = \Delta t_i,

\mathbb{E}\!\Big[\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big] \;=\; \sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i

Letting the mesh \|\Pi\| \to 0 (a Riemann sum),

\mathbb{E}\!\Big[\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big] \;=\; \sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i \;\xrightarrow{\|\Pi\| \to 0}\; \int_0^t f(s)\, ds

Variance: By independence the variances add, and each deterministic factor comes out squared,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big) \;=\; \sum_i f(t_i)^2\, \operatorname{Var}\big((\Delta W_i)^2\big)

Substituting \operatorname{Var}\big((\Delta W_i)^2\big) = 2(\Delta t_i)^2,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big) \;=\; 2 \sum_i f(t_i)^2\, (\Delta t_i)^2

Bounding f(t_i)^2 \le \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big) \;\le\; 2\big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2 \sum_i (\Delta t_i)^2

Bounding \sum_i (\Delta t_i)^2 \le \|\Pi\|\, t by the mesh,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big) \;\le\; 2\big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2\, \|\Pi\|\, t

Letting the mesh \|\Pi\| \to 0,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, (\Delta W_i)^2\Big) \;\le\; 2\big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2\, \|\Pi\|\, t \;\xrightarrow{\|\Pi\| \to 0}\; 0

A random variable whose mean converges to \int_0^t f(s)\, ds and whose variance vanishes converges in L^2 to that limit, since \mathbb{E}\big[(S - \int_0^t f\, ds)^2\big] = \operatorname{Var}(S) + \big(\mathbb{E}[S] - \int_0^t f\, ds\big)^2 and both terms vanish. So the sum converges to \int_0^t f(s)\, ds — which is exactly the value Equation 4 asserts. \square Setting f \equiv 1 specializes it to the plain quadratic variation Equation 2. So whenever (dW)^2 appears inside a stochastic integral, we may substitute dt for it — the two integrals agree in the limit, as Itô’s lemma will use the rule.


1.7.2 Companion rules
Two further rules,

\boxed{(dt)^2 = 0}
\tag{5}

\boxed{dt\,dW = 0}
\tag{6}
follow by the same partition-sum reasoning, established next.

1.7.2.1 The (dt)^2 rule is deterministic
This rule carries no randomness, so a single deterministic bound suffices — but the weight f may change sign, so the bound must control the sum in absolute value. By the triangle inequality,

\Big|\sum_i f(t_i)\,(\Delta t_i)^2\Big| \;\le\; \sum_i |f(t_i)|\,(\Delta t_i)^2

Bounding the weight by |f(t_i)| \le \sup_{[0,t]}|f|,

\Big|\sum_i f(t_i)\,(\Delta t_i)^2\Big| \;\le\; \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big) \sum_i (\Delta t_i)^2

Bounding \sum_i (\Delta t_i)^2 \le \|\Pi\|\, t by the mesh,

\Big|\sum_i f(t_i)\,(\Delta t_i)^2\Big| \;\le\; \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)\, \|\Pi\|\, t

Letting the mesh \|\Pi\| \to 0,

\Big|\sum_i f(t_i)\,(\Delta t_i)^2\Big| \;\le\; \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)\, \|\Pi\|\, t \;\xrightarrow{\|\Pi\| \to 0}\; 0

The bound is deterministic — no randomness enters — and it squeezes the partition sum to zero in absolute value as the mesh refines, so the sum itself converges to zero, giving the integral form

\int_0^t f(s)\,(ds)^2 = 0

whose equivalent differential form is (dt)^2 = 0, Equation 5.


1.7.2.2 The dt\,dW rule is an L^2 statement
The partition sum \sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i has mean zero, since each \Delta W_i is mean-zero. For its variance, the increments are independent across non-overlapping intervals, so variances add and each deterministic factor comes out squared,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\Big) \;=\; \sum_i f(t_i)^2\, (\Delta t_i)^2\, \operatorname{Var}(\Delta W_i)

Substituting \operatorname{Var}(\Delta W_i) = \Delta t_i,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\Big) \;=\; \sum_i f(t_i)^2\, (\Delta t_i)^3

Bounding f(t_i)^2 \le \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\Big) \;\le\; \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2 \sum_i (\Delta t_i)^3

Bounding two of the three factors of each (\Delta t_i)^3 by the mesh, (\Delta t_i)^2 \le \|\Pi\|^2,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\Big) \;\le\; \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2\, \|\Pi\|^2 \sum_i \Delta t_i

Telescoping \sum_i \Delta t_i = t,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\Big) \;\le\; \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2\, \|\Pi\|^2\, t

Letting the mesh \|\Pi\| \to 0,

\operatorname{Var}\!\Big(\sum_i f(t_i)\, \Delta t_i\, \Delta W_i\Big) \;\le\; \big(\sup_{[0,t]}|f|\big)^2\, \|\Pi\|^2\, t \;\xrightarrow{\|\Pi\| \to 0}\; 0

The partition sum thus has mean zero and a variance vanishing to zero as the mesh refines. A sequence with mean zero whose variance tends to zero converges to zero in L^2 (mean square), so the partition sum converges in L^2 to zero, giving the integral form

\int_0^t f(s)\, ds\, dW_s = 0

whose equivalent differential form is dt\,dW = 0, Equation 6.
So only (dW)^2 survives at first order in dt — and what survives, by Equation 4, is dt.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
section: 1.8 The Itô integral: a Gaussian under L^2
text:
1.8 The Itô integral: a Gaussian under L^2
The same partition-sum construction determines one more object used throughout: the Itô integral of a deterministic function against Brownian motion, \int_0^t g(s)\, dW_s := \lim_{\|\Pi\| \to 0} \sum_i g(t_i)\, \Delta W_i — the left-endpoint limit of partition sums, as in Equation 4 but now linear in \Delta W_i instead of (\Delta W_i)^2. Defining it rigorously for general random integrands is carried out in Appendix A.4 [6]; the deterministic case is all this post needs, and there the Wiener increment structure alone fixes the full distribution.
For deterministic g,

\boxed{\int_0^t g(s)\, dW_s \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(0,\;\; \int_0^t g(s)^2\, ds\right)}
\tag{7}
Why: Approximate the integral by a partition sum \sum_i g(t_i)\, \Delta W_i, with independent increments \Delta W_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Delta t_i). A finite linear combination of independent Gaussians is Gaussian, so each partition sum is Gaussian; its mean vanishes term by term, and by independence its variance is \sum_i g(t_i)^2\, \Delta t_i \to \int_0^t g(s)^2\, ds (a Riemann sum, g continuous).
As \|\Pi\| \to 0 the sums converge in L^2 to the integral — the same convergence used for Equation 4. Because L^2 convergence carries the mean and variance to the limit, the limit has mean 0 and variance \int_0^t g^2\, ds; and a mean-square limit of Gaussians is itself Gaussian — the Gaussian family is closed under L^2 limits, proved in Appendix A.6 — so the integral is Gaussian. The variance identity is the Itô isometry; the zero mean follows from the martingale property of the Itô integral.
Martingale property: (made precise in Appendix A.5) A martingale is a process with no systematic trend — given everything observed up to the present, its expected future value equals its present value. The Itô integral M_t = \int_0^t g(s)\, dW_s is one, and since it starts at M_0 = 0, taking expectations gives \mathbb{E}[M_t] = 0 for every t — on average it neither rises nor falls. This is the zero-mean half of Equation 7.
Itô isometry: An isometry is a map that preserves size. The map g \mapsto \int_0^t g\, dW_s sends a function to a random variable while preserving the L^2 norm: \mathbb{E}\big[\big(\int_0^t g(s)\, dW_s\big)^2\big] = \int_0^t g(s)^2\, ds — the mean-square size of the integral equals the ordinary size of the integrand. This is the variance half of Equation 7.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
2.1 Stochastic differential equations
Brownian motion is pure, undirected noise — mean-zero increments whose variance accumulates at unit rate (Equation 2). Real systems rarely behave so simply: a stock price exhibits a trend, a temperature relaxes toward ambient, a population grows — each carrying its own deterministic tendency while still being buffeted by randomness, often responding to that noise with an intensity that depends on the current state. To describe such a process we specify not its value but its instantaneous change — a deterministic push over dt plus a scaled increment of W_t — and let those infinitesimal updates accumulate into a path.
A (one-dimensional) Itô SDE has the form

\boxed{dX_t = \mu(X_t, t)\, dt + \sigma(X_t, t)\, dW_t}
\tag{8}
where \mu is the drift coefficient and \sigma is the diffusion coefficient. The notation dX_t, dt, dW_t is shorthand for the integral equation

\boxed{X_t = X_0 + \int_0^t \mu(X_s, s)\, ds + \int_0^t \sigma(X_s, s)\, dW_s}
\tag{9}
where the second integral is the Itô integral of Section 1.8. There the integrand is deterministic; here \sigma(X_s, s) is generally state-dependent and therefore random, but the same heuristic form is all this post needs.
The drift term governs the deterministic evolution of X_t; the diffusion term governs the size of random fluctuations. Conditions under which such an SDE has a unique solution — global Lipschitz and linear growth on \mu and \sigma — are stated and proved in Appendix A.1 of post #2; every process in this series satisfies them.
The next two subsections introduce two concrete instances of this form — geometric Brownian motion (GBM) and the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process — each obtained by choosing the drift and diffusion coefficients \mu(x,t) and \sigma(x,t). We solve both later with Itô’s lemma (GBM in Section 2.4.1, the OU process in Section 2.4.2), and both recur downstream: the former as the Black-Scholes stock model in Part 3, the latter as the template for the DDPM forward process in Part 4.

2.1.1 Geometric Brownian Motion (GBM)
In the Black-Scholes framework, S_t denotes the price of a stock at time t, and is modeled by the SDE

\boxed{dS_t \;=\; \mu\, S_t\, dt \;+\; \sigma\, S_t\, dW_t}
\tag{10}
with scalar constants \mu, \sigma. This is Equation 8 with drift coefficient \mu(x, t) = \mu\, x and diffusion coefficient \sigma(x, t) = \sigma\, x — both linear in x. (The symbols \mu, \sigma are reused here as scalar constants, distinct from the coefficient functions \mu(x,t), \sigma(x,t) of Equation 8 — standard finance notation.)
The parameters have precise finance meanings:

Drift (\mu): The instantaneous expected rate of return per unit time, \mathbb{E}[dS_t/S_t] = \mu\, dt. \mu = 0.15 means a 15\% per-year expected return (with t measured in years); the continuously-compounded growth rate is the smaller \mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 (the Itô correction, derived below).
Volatility (\sigma): The standard deviation of the return per unit time. \sigma = 0.20 means 20\% per-year volatility.









Figure 6: Sample paths of geometric Brownian motion with \mu = 0.15, \sigma = 0.35, S_0 = 1 over one year (a larger \sigma than the 0.20 example in the text, chosen so the skew below is visible). The dashed line is the deterministic expected value \mathbb{E}[S_t] = S_0\, e^{\mu t}. Paths trend upward in expectation but remain strictly positive throughout. The right panel is the marginal distribution of the endpoint S_1 (histogram of many paths, analytic density in rose): it is lognormal — right-skewed with a long upper tail and bounded below by zero — the property guaranteed by the model and derived in Section 2.4.1.





Sample paths trend upward in expectation while remaining strictly positive (Figure 6). We solve this SDE for the full distribution of S_t — applying Itô’s lemma to \log S_t — in Section 2.4.1, where the price is shown to be log-normally distributed.


2.1.2 Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process
The OU process [7] is the canonical mean-reverting SDE. With state X_t \in \mathbb{R}, long-run mean \bar\mu, mean-reversion rate \theta > 0, and constant volatility \sigma > 0,

\boxed{dX_t \;=\; \theta\,(\bar\mu - X_t)\, dt \;+\; \sigma\, dW_t}
\tag{11}
This is Equation 8 with drift coefficient \theta(\bar\mu - x) (linear in x, restoring toward \bar\mu) and constant diffusion \sigma (independent of x).
The parameters:

Long-run mean (\bar\mu): The value the process is pulled toward.
Mean-reversion rate (\theta): Units 1/\text{time}; larger \theta pulls harder. The expected excursion decays as e^{-\theta t} (Equation 17, derived in Section 2.4.2), so its “half-life” — the time to halve — is \ln 2 / \theta.
Volatility (\sigma): The constant volatility of the noise, units \text{state}/\sqrt{\text{time}}.

The mean-reversion intuition: If X_t > \bar\mu, the drift \theta(\bar\mu - X_t) < 0 pushes X_t back down. If X_t < \bar\mu, the drift pushes it back up. The noise term \sigma\, dW_t keeps the process jittering around \bar\mu rather than converging to it (Figure 7).








Figure 7: Sample paths of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with long-run mean \bar\mu = 0, mean-reversion rate \theta = 1, and volatility \sigma = 0.5, started from several different points. Whatever the start, the drift pulls every path into the same stationary band \bar\mu \pm \sqrt{\sigma^2/(2\theta)} (shaded) around \bar\mu (dashed). The right panel is a histogram of one long run: the paths settle into the stationary distribution \mathcal{N}(0,\, \sigma^2/2\theta) (solid curve), independent of where they began.





Stationary distribution: Unlike GBM — whose spread grows without bound (its log-return variance is \sigma^2 t, derived in Section 2.4.1) — OU has a finite-variance equilibrium. As t \to \infty,

\boxed{X_t \;\xrightarrow{\text{dist}}\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(\bar\mu,\;\, \frac{\sigma^2}{2\theta}\right)}
\tag{12}
The equilibrium variance \sigma^2/(2\theta) arises from the balance between noise injection (\sigma) and restoring force (\theta): more noise widens the spread, stronger reversion tightens it. The full derivation — solving the SDE by an integrating factor and letting t \to \infty — is in Section 2.4.2 after Itô’s lemma is introduced.
Where OU shows up:

In finance:

In interest-rate modeling, the Vasicek model [8] treats the instantaneous risk-free rate as an OU process.
In statistical-arbitrage, cointegrated price spreads — the difference between two related instruments — are modeled as mean-reverting OU processes.

In generative AI:

OU is the simplest non-trivial Langevin-style SDE: it samples its Gaussian equilibrium \mathcal{N}(\bar\mu,\, \sigma^2/(2\theta)) by mean reversion plus noise, and the same drift-plus-noise template lets Langevin dynamics sample any target distribution (post #4).
The reverse, generative process of DDPM is that template generalized — a learned, time-dependent score \nabla_x \log p_t replaces OU’s fixed linear drift, turning pure noise back into data (post #2).

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
2.2 Itô’s lemma
The SDEs of Section 2.1 describe how a state X_t evolves; the question of interest is how functions of that state move. Given dX_t = \mu\,dt + \sigma\,dW_t, what SDE governs a transformed quantity Y_t = f(X_t, t) — a log-price, an option value, a noise schedule? For a smooth, deterministic X the ordinary chain rule would answer at once, but it fails here: the (dW)^2 = dt rule of Equation 3 means a second-order term that classical calculus discards instead survives at order dt. Itô’s lemma resolves this — it is the ordinary chain rule plus exactly one correction term.
Let X_t satisfy the SDE dX_t = \mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW_t, and let f(x, t) be a function that is twice continuously differentiable in x and once in t. Then according to Itô’s lemma the process Y_t = f(X_t, t) satisfies [9], [10]

\boxed{df = \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + \mu \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\right) dt + \sigma \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dW}
\tag{13}
The term \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\, dt is the Itô correction. It is what distinguishes Itô calculus from ordinary calculus.

2.2.1 Derivation
Taylor-expand f(X_{t+dt}, t+dt) to second order in x and first order in t — all the smoothness f is assumed to possess; the omitted higher terms are of order dt \cdot dX and (dt)^2, which the companion rules Equation 6 and Equation 5 annihilate:

df \;=\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt \;+\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dX \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\, (dX)^2

Substituting dX = \mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW,

df \;=\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt \;+\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,(\mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\, (\mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW)^2

Expanding the square,

df \;=\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt \;+\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,(\mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\,\bigl(\mu^2 (dt)^2 + 2\mu\sigma\, dt\, dW + \sigma^2 (dW)^2\bigr)

Reducing the squared increment via the companion rules (dt)^2 = 0, dt\,dW = 0, (dW)^2 = dt,

df \;=\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt \;+\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,(\mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\, dt

Distributing \partial f / \partial x across the bracket,

df \;=\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\, dt \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dt \;+\; \sigma\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dW \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\, dt

Grouping by dt and dW gives,

\boxed{df \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\right) dt \;+\; \sigma\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dW}

which is Equation 13. \square


2.2.2 Comparison to the chain rule
Suppose we naively applied the ordinary chain rule to a stochastic X with dX = \mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW — substitute dX, stop at first order as we do in the ordinary case. We’d write

df \;\stackrel{?}{=}\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right) dt \;+\; \sigma\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dW

That is what ordinary calculus would give — and in Itô calculus it is the wrong answer. Itô’s lemma is character-for-character the same, except for one extra term in the dt coefficient:

df \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \;+\; \underbrace{\boxed{\tfrac{1}{2}\,\sigma^2\,\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}}}_{\text{Itô correction — the square term}}\right) dt \;+\; \sigma\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dW

The boxed second-order term is the only structural difference between the two equations. Every other character matches the naive chain rule. It is the surviving term from the (dW)^2 = dt rule of Equation 3 — that partition-sum identity, promoted to a calculus correction.


2.2.3 The deterministic limit (\sigma \to 0)
A correct stochastic chain rule must reduce to the ordinary one when the noise is switched off — that is the sanity check.
Set \sigma = 0. The SDE loses its diffusion term,

dX_t = \mu\, dt

so X is now a smooth (differentiable) path with derivative \dot X = dX_t / dt = \mu.
For a smooth path, Y_t = f(X_t, t) changes for two reasons: f depends on t directly, and it depends on t through X_t. The ordinary multivariable chain rule sums the two contributions — the explicit rate \partial f / \partial t, and the rate transmitted through X moving at speed \dot X, namely \dot X\, \partial f / \partial x:

\frac{dY}{dt} \;=\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \dot X\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}

Substituting \dot X = \mu,

\frac{dY}{dt} \;=\; \frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}

Multiplying by dt,

dY \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right) dt

Now set \sigma = 0 in Itô’s lemma. Starting from the full result,

df \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\right) dt \;+\; \sigma\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\, dW

Setting \sigma = 0 — the second-order term \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2\, \partial^2 f / \partial x^2 and the \sigma\, \partial f / \partial x\, dW term both vanish —

df \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right) dt

The two agree exactly: with no noise, Itô’s lemma is the ordinary chain rule. The second-order term is what the (dW)^2 = dt rule adds once \sigma \neq 0.
Thus, Itô’s lemma = ordinary chain rule + (dW)^2 = dt correction.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
2.3 Application patterns of Itô’s lemma
Two patterns will recur. In one, we follow the path a particle takes once it starts moving; in the other, we track the probability-density cloud, estimating how likely the particle is to be at a given place and time after its journey begins. Specifically, Pattern A rides along a single trajectory: it transforms one SDE into another, tracking some function of the moving state. Pattern B steps back to ask, at each time and place, how likely the state is to be there: it turns the SDE into a PDE for the probability density. Same lemma, same SDE — one follows the path, the other predicts the distribution. These are the two views of one diffusion introduced in Section 1.1, now made into two ways of applying the lemma.
Pattern A: Given an SDE for X_t, derive an SDE for a transformed quantity f(X_t, t). It recurs in every part that follows:

Section 2.4.1: f(S) = \log S applied to the GBM stock price gives its closed-form lognormal distribution.
Section 2.4.2: The integrating-factor transform f(Z, t) = e^{\theta t} Z applied to the long-run-mean-centered OU process gives its closed-form Gaussian distribution.
Section 3.3 - Section 3.7: f = V(S, t) applied to the GBM stock price yields the Black-Scholes PDE.
Section 4.9: A similar integrating-factor transform f(x, t) = x / \sqrt{\bar\alpha(t)} applied to the DDPM VP-SDE turns it into a driftless process, giving its closed-form Gaussian law — the perturbation kernel.

Pattern B: Given an SDE for X_t, derive a PDE for its probability density p(x, t) — the Fokker-Planck equation. It appears once:

Section 4.10: Applying Itô to a test function and taking expectations turns the VP-SDE into the Fokker-Planck equation for its marginal distribution p(x, t), giving the PDE that governs how the DDPM forward process spreads the data density into noise over time.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
section: 2.4 Itô’s lemma solves GBM and the OU process
text:
2.4 Itô’s lemma solves GBM and the OU process
Itô’s lemma is most convincing in action. We turn it on the two example SDEs from Section 2.1 — GBM and the OU process — and in each case a single application collapses a state-dependent SDE into one we can integrate in closed form.

2.4.1 Solving GBM
We solve GBM for the full distribution of the price S_t by applying Itô’s lemma to the transform f(S) = \log S — a function of S alone, with no explicit time dependence. (\log S requires S_t > 0, so the step is valid while the price stays positive; the resulting solution Equation 14 is an exponential, strictly positive for all t, which closes the loop on that assumption.)

2.4.1.1 Use Itô to get reduced SDE
The SDE: The price S_t follows the GBM SDE Equation 10,

dS_t \;=\; \mu\, S_t\, dt \;+\; \sigma\, S_t\, dW_t

Itô’s lemma: To avoid clashing with the GBM constants \mu, \sigma, write the generic lemma with drift coefficient a and diffusion coefficient b — that is, for a transform f(S_t, t) of a process dS_t = a\, dt + b\, dW_t, the lemma Equation 13 reads

df \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; a\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial S} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, b^2\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial S^2}\right) dt \;+\; b\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial S}\, dW

To apply it to f = \log S we need two elements: the coefficients a, b — identified from the GBM equation — and the partials of f — computed from f = \log S. We collect each, then substitute.
Coefficients (from the GBM equation): a = \mu\, S_t and b = \sigma\, S_t.
Partials (from f = \log S):

\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;=\; 0, \qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial S} \;=\; \frac{1}{S}, \qquad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial S^2} \;=\; -\frac{1}{S^2}

Substituting a = \mu\, S, b = \sigma\, S, and the three partials into the lemma,

d(\log S_t) \;=\; \left(0 \;+\; (\mu\, S) \cdot \frac{1}{S} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, (\sigma\, S)^2 \cdot \left(-\frac{1}{S^2}\right)\right) dt \;+\; (\sigma\, S) \cdot \frac{1}{S}\, dW_t

Simplifying,

d(\log S_t) \;=\; \left(\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\right) dt + \sigma\, dW_t

a constant-drift, constant-diffusion SDE: both coefficients are independent of S_t.


2.4.1.2 Solve reduced SDE by integration
Integrating this reduced SDE over [0, t],

\log\!\left(\frac{S_t}{S_0}\right) \;=\; \big(\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\big)\, t \;+\; \sigma \int_0^t dW_s

Since W_0 = 0, the Itô integral is \int_0^t dW_s = W_t,

\boxed{\log\!\left(\frac{S_t}{S_0}\right) \;=\; \big(\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\big)\, t \;+\; \sigma\, W_t}
\tag{14}


2.4.1.3 Properties of the solution distribution
Since W_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, t), the log-return is an affine function of a Gaussian — hence Gaussian:

\boxed{\log\!\left(\frac{S_t}{S_0}\right) \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\Big(\, \big(\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\big)\, t,\;\; \sigma^2\, t \,\Big)}
\tag{15}
Taking expectations of S_t = S_0\, e^{(\mu - \sigma^2/2)t + \sigma W_t}, with the deterministic factor pulled out,

\mathbb{E}[S_t] = S_0\, e^{(\mu - \sigma^2/2)t}\, \mathbb{E}[e^{\sigma W_t}]

Applying the Gaussian moment \mathbb{E}[e^{\sigma W_t}] = e^{\sigma^2 t/2},

\mathbb{E}[S_t] = S_0\, e^{\mu t}

The level grows at the full rate \mu even as the typical log-return grows at \mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2.
So log-returns have mean (\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)\, t and variance \sigma^2 t — variance linear in time (characteristic of Brownian motion), so the standard deviation grows like \sigma\sqrt{t}. Equivalently, the price S_t itself is log-normally distributed: its logarithm is Gaussian, which forces S_t > 0 always — essential, because stock prices can’t go negative.
The -\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 term is the Itô correction in action (Figure 8). Naive chain-rule reasoning would give d(\log S) = dS/S = \mu\, dt + \sigma\, dW — missing the -\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\, dt contribution that the (dW)^2 = dt rule supplies. The mean of the log-return is therefore not \mu\, t but (\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)\, t; the gap is sometimes referred to in finance as the volatility drag.








Figure 8: The Itô correction, numerically. A single geometric Brownian motion path (\mu = 0.10, \sigma = 0.40) is generated by Euler–Maruyama on dS = \mu S\, dt + \sigma S\, dW — the log-formula is not assumed — and then logged. The naive chain rule would predict \log(S_t/S_0) = \mu t + \sigma W_t, but the simulated log-return instead tracks (\mu - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)\, t + \sigma W_t. Both are driven by the same noise W_t, so they move in lockstep yet separate at the steady rate \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2: the shaded wedge is exactly the -\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 t correction the naive rule omits.








2.4.2 Solving the OU process
The OU process Equation 11 is the mean-reverting counterpart, and the same lemma determines its long-run law. We solve it in closed form and recover the stationary distribution Equation 12.

2.4.2.1 Use Itô to get reduced SDE
The SDE: The OU process Equation 11 is

dX_t \;=\; \theta\,(\bar\mu - X_t)\, dt \;+\; \sigma\, dW_t

Centering on its long-run mean, Z_t = X_t - \bar\mu, so that the SDE becomes

dZ_t \;=\; -\theta\, Z_t\, dt \;+\; \sigma\, dW_t

Itô’s lemma: For a transform f(Z_t, t) of a process with drift coefficient a and diffusion coefficient b — that is, dZ_t = a\, dt + b\, dW_t — the lemma Equation 13 reads

df \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;+\; a\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial Z} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, b^2\, \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial Z^2}\right) dt \;+\; b\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial Z}\, dW

Integrating factor: The standard technique for a linear SDE is to apply Itô’s lemma to the transform Y_t = f(Z_t, t) with f(Z, t) = e^{\theta t} Z — chosen so the explicit-time term cancels the drift.
Coefficients (from the centered SDE): a = -\theta\, Z_t and b = \sigma.
Partials (from f = e^{\theta t} Z):

\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \;=\; \theta\, e^{\theta t} Z, \qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial Z} \;=\; e^{\theta t}, \qquad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial Z^2} \;=\; 0

Substituting a = -\theta\, Z, b = \sigma, and the three partials into the lemma,

d\!\left(e^{\theta t} Z_t\right) \;=\; \Big(\theta\, e^{\theta t} Z \;+\; (-\theta\, Z)\, e^{\theta t} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2 \cdot 0\Big) dt \;+\; \sigma\, e^{\theta t}\, dW_t

Simplifying — the explicit-time term \theta\, e^{\theta t} Z and the drift term -\theta\, e^{\theta t} Z cancel,

d\!\left(e^{\theta t} Z_t\right) \;=\; \sigma\, e^{\theta t}\, dW_t



2.4.2.2 Solve reduced SDE by integration
Integrating from 0 to t,

\int_0^t d\!\left(e^{\theta s} Z_s\right) \;=\; \sigma \int_0^t e^{\theta s}\, dW_s

Evaluating the left side, \int_0^t d\!\left(e^{\theta s} Z_s\right) = e^{\theta t} Z_t - Z_0,

e^{\theta t} Z_t \;=\; Z_0 \;+\; \sigma \int_0^t e^{\theta s}\, dW_s

As Z_0 = X_0 - \bar\mu,

e^{\theta t} Z_t \;=\; (X_0 - \bar\mu) \;+\; \sigma \int_0^t e^{\theta s}\, dW_s

Dividing by e^{\theta t},

Z_t \;=\; (X_0 - \bar\mu)\, e^{-\theta t} \;+\; \sigma \int_0^t e^{-\theta(t - s)}\, dW_s

Substituting Z_t = X_t - \bar\mu,

\boxed{X_t \;=\; \bar\mu \;+\; (X_0 - \bar\mu)\, e^{-\theta t} \;+\; \sigma \int_0^t e^{-\theta(t - s)}\, dW_s}
\tag{16}


2.4.2.3 Properties of the solution distribution
Given X_0, the offset \bar\mu + (X_0 - \bar\mu)e^{-\theta t} is a deterministic constant, and the Itô integral is Gaussian by Equation 7; adding the constant leaves X_t an affine function of that Gaussian, and an affine function of a Gaussian is Gaussian.
Mean: The Itô integral has zero mean by Equation 7, so

\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X_t] \;=\; \bar\mu \;+\; (X_0 - \bar\mu)\, e^{-\theta t}}
\tag{17}
Variance: By Equation 7 with g(s) = \sigma\, e^{-\theta(t - s)},

\operatorname{Var}[X_t] \;=\; \sigma^2 \int_0^t e^{-2\theta(t - s)}\, ds

Evaluating the integral,

\boxed{\operatorname{Var}[X_t] \;=\; \frac{\sigma^2}{2\theta}\big(1 - e^{-2\theta t}\big)}
\tag{18}
Stationary distribution: As t \to \infty the decaying exponentials vanish — e^{-\theta t} \to 0 in the mean and e^{-2\theta t} \to 0 in the variance — so \mathbb{E}[X_t] \to \bar\mu and \operatorname{Var}[X_t] \to \sigma^2/(2\theta). Since X_t is Gaussian for every t, its law converges to

\boxed{\mathcal{N}\!\left(\bar\mu,\;\, \frac{\sigma^2}{2\theta}\right)}

which is Equation 12. \square

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
3.1 What is an option?
An option is a contract whose value depends on — is derived from — the price of an underlying stock S_t. The contract grants its holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an agreed quantity of the stock at a pre-agreed price per stock (strike, K) at a specified maturity (T). The two basic types are:

Call option: Confers its buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy an agreed quantity of the stock at the strike price K at maturity T.
Put option: Confers its buyer the right, but not the obligation, to sell an agreed quantity of the stock at the strike price K at maturity T.

American options can be exercised at any time up to maturity T while European options can be exercised only at the maturity T. This post restricts attention to European options; American options require additional theory beyond the present scope.
Payoff at expiry: At t = T, the option’s value depends only on S_T. A rational holder exercises the option only when doing so is profitable, giving the piecewise-linear payoff functions:
The call payoff is

\boxed{V_{\text{call}}(S_T) = \max(S_T - K,\, 0)}
\tag{20}
The holder exercises if S_T > K, gaining S_T - K; otherwise the option expires worthless.
The put payoff is

\boxed{V_{\text{put}}(S_T) = \max(K - S_T,\, 0)}
\tag{21}
The holder exercises if S_T < K, gaining K - S_T; otherwise the option expires worthless.
The kinked “hockey-stick” shape (Figure 9) is the structural signature of an option: identically zero on the unfavourable side of the strike, linear on the favourable side.








Figure 9: Payoff at expiry t = T for European call (left) and put (right) options with strike K = 100. The call holder exercises only if S_T > K, receiving S_T - K; the put holder exercises only if S_T < K, receiving K - S_T. The kinked ‘hockey-stick’ shape — flat on the unfavourable side of the strike, linear on the favourable side — is the structural signature of an option.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
3.2 Key finance terms

Risk-free rate: The interest rate an investor can expect to earn on an investment that carries zero risk. In practice, usually the interest paid on a 10-year highly rated government Treasury note.
Risky asset: An instrument whose future price is uncertain, evolving stochastically. In other words, the diffusion coefficient \sigma(x, t) in its dynamics will not be 0. For example, a stock.
Risk-free asset: An instrument whose return is known in advance, carrying no price uncertainty. In other words, the diffusion coefficient \sigma(x, t) in its dynamics will be 0. For example, a bank account; a unit of cash held in it grows deterministically at the risk-free rate.
Long / short positions: Holding +q units of an instrument is being long q; owing q units (selling now, buying back later) is being short q (a negative position, -q). A long position profits when the price rises; a short position profits when it falls.
Portfolio: A collection of financial investments such as stocks, bonds, and options. If a portfolio has i = 1, \dots, n instruments and the quantity and price of the ith instrument are q_i and P_i respectively, the portfolio value \Pi_t is 
\Pi_t = \sum_{i=1}^{n} q_i\, P_i

Delta: The sensitivity of an instrument’s value to a one-unit change in the stock price — the partial derivative of that value with respect to S.
Portfolio delta: The sensitivity of the portfolio value to a one-unit change in the stock price, \partial \Pi / \partial S. Distributing the partial derivative through the sum, 
\frac{\partial \Pi}{\partial S} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} q_i\, \frac{\partial P_i}{\partial S}

Delta-neutral: A portfolio with zero portfolio delta, \partial \Pi / \partial S = 0 — the quantities q_i are chosen so the deltas of the instruments held cancel, leaving no delta exposure, so the portfolio is immune to a change in the stock price to first order.
Self-financing strategy: A trading approach where a portfolio’s value changes only due to gains or losses from its assets, with no external cash inflows or withdrawals.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
3.3 The option value process
Given the terminal payoff of Equation 20 as the boundary condition, pricing the option requires finding the SDE its value obeys — and Itô’s lemma provides it, applied to V(S, t) under the same GBM stock dynamics we used for \log S in Section 2.4.1.
Let V(S, t) denote the per-share value of a European call option on S with strike K and maturity T. (Real option contracts typically represent multiple shares; the pricing is done per share throughout this derivation and scales linearly with quantity.) Assume V is twice continuously differentiable in S and once in t for t < T — the hypothesis of Equation 13; the closed-form solution of Section 3.7.1 confirms it for the call, the payoff’s kink at S = K smoothing out instantly for t < T. Apply Itô’s lemma to V under the GBM dynamics of Equation 10 (constant drift \mu, constant volatility \sigma; adopted as the Part 3 stock model in Section 2.4.1):

dV = \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} + \mu S \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}\right) dt + \sigma S \frac{\partial V}{\partial S}\, dW_t
\tag{22}
The challenge that Black-Scholes addresses is the prior question: given today’s price S_t and the stock-price dynamics, what is the fair value V(S_t, t) of the option before expiry, for t < T? Itô’s lemma combined with a delta-neutral, risk-free portfolio of the stock and the option produces a PDE for V whose boundary condition is the terminal call payoff V(S, T) = \max(S - K,\, 0) (Equation 20).

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
3.4 Black-Scholes assumptions
The Black-Scholes derivation [11], [12] rests on a specific set of idealising assumptions about the market and the assets traded in it. Collecting them upfront makes both the construction and its limitations transparent.

3.4.1 Market structure
The market consists of two instruments:

A risk-free asset — a bank account or zero-coupon bond.
A risky asset — a single stock with price S_t.



3.4.2 Assumptions on the assets

Risk-free asset dynamics: The risk-free asset B_t earns a continuously-compounded rate r that does not vary with time, 
dB_t = r\, B_t\, dt
 Being risk-free, its diffusion term is 0 — there is no dW_t — so its value grows deterministically as B_t = B_0\, e^{rt}.
Stock dynamics: The stock price follows the GBM dynamics of Equation 10, with constant drift \mu and constant volatility \sigma, 
dS_t = \mu\, S_t\, dt + \sigma\, S_t\, dW_t
 Here the diffusion term is not 0: the \sigma\, S_t\, dW_t term is the source of the stock’s uncertainty, and is what makes it risky.
No dividends: The stock pays no dividends over [t, T].



3.4.3 Assumptions on the market

No arbitrage: No strategy delivers a risk-free profit in excess of r. Equivalently, any two portfolios with identical payoffs in every future scenario must have identical prices today.
Frictionless trading: Transactions are executed instantaneously with no fees, no bid–ask spread, no taxes, and no market impact. Continuous-time trading is permitted.
Unlimited borrowing and lending at r: Cash may be borrowed or lent in any real-valued amount at the risk-free rate.
Unrestricted stock positions: Any real-valued quantity of the stock may be held, including short positions (negative quantities), with no borrowing cost or quantity constraint.

The assumptions above are idealisations — real markets violate every one of them to some degree. Their utility is conceptual: under these conditions, the derivative-pricing problem reduces to a well-posed PDE with a known closed-form solution.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
3.5 Black-Scholes pricing strategy
Given a European option with terminal payoff V(S, T) = \max(S - K,\, 0) (Equation 20) and the option-value SDE Equation 22, the remaining argument unfolds in three steps:

Form a hedged portfolio: Construct a portfolio by holding +1 unit of the call option and -\Delta_t units of the stock, giving 
\Pi_t = V(S_t, t) - \Delta_t\, S_t
 The dW_t contributions from dV and from \Delta_t\, dS_t cancel exactly, rendering the portfolio instantaneously risk-free. (Section 3.6)
Invoke no-arbitrage: A risk-free portfolio must earn the risk-free rate: d\Pi_t = r\, \Pi_t\, dt. Equating this with the deterministic dynamics from Step 1 yields a PDE for V(S, t) — the Black-Scholes PDE. (Section 3.7)
Solve the PDE: Solving the PDE using the boundary condition V(S, T) = \max(S - K,\, 0) (Equation 20) gives the Black-Scholes pricing formula for a European call.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
3.6 The hedging portfolio
We want to hold the option together with something else so that the combined position is delta-neutral — its value insensitive to small moves in the stock price. Of the other instruments in the market, the risk-free asset has zero delta and cannot offset S-exposure, so the stock is the only candidate: hold the option long and a quantity q_t of the stock, with q_t to be determined:

\Pi_t = V(S_t, t) + q_t\, S_t

Its portfolio delta is the sensitivity of \Pi_t to the stock price, computed from this definition (treating q_t as constant in S at the instant t):

\frac{\partial \Pi_t}{\partial S} = \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} + q_t
\tag{23}
Delta-neutrality requires \partial \Pi_t/\partial S = 0, which forces q_t = -\partial V/\partial S = -\Delta_t, where \Delta_t = \partial V/\partial S is the option’s delta (defined in Section 3.2). So delta-neutrality fixes the stock position: hold the option long and short \Delta_t units of the stock.
Thus, to make the portfolio delta-neutral and risk-free we hold the option long and short \Delta_t = \partial V/\partial S units of the stock:

\Pi_t = V(S_t, t) - \Delta_t S_t
\tag{24}
Over an infinitesimal interval, the portfolio changes by

d\Pi_t = dV - \Delta_t\, dS_t

Writing it this way drops the -S_t\, d\Delta_t - d\Delta_t\, dS_t terms that the Itô product rule adds for a time-varying \Delta_t. This is not an approximation: the hedge is run as a self-financing strategy, so the cash released or absorbed by rebalancing the stock position is exactly offset by a cash account and nets to zero in d\Pi_t over [t, t+dt] — the accounting is in Appendix A.3.
Step 1 — substitute the option change:
Substituting Equation 22 (Itô’s lemma applied to V) for dV,

d\Pi_t \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu S\, \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2 S^2\, \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}\right) dt \;+\; \sigma S\, \frac{\partial V}{\partial S}\, dW_t \;-\; \Delta_t\, dS_t

Step 2 — substitute the stock change:
Substituting Equation 10, dS_t = \mu S\, dt + \sigma S\, dW_t,

d\Pi_t \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu S\, \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2 S^2\, \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}\right) dt \;+\; \sigma S\, \frac{\partial V}{\partial S}\, dW_t \;-\; \Delta_t\, \mu S\, dt \;-\; \Delta_t\, \sigma S\, dW_t

Step 3 — collect like differentials:
Grouping the dt terms and the dW_t terms,

d\Pi_t \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu S\, \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} \;-\; \Delta_t\, \mu S \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2 S^2\, \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}\right) dt \;+\; \left(\sigma S\, \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} \;-\; \Delta_t\, \sigma S\right) dW_t

Step 4 — factor the paired terms:
Factoring \mu S out of the drift pair and \sigma S out of the dW_t pair,

d\Pi_t \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} \;+\; \mu S \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial S} - \Delta_t\right) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2 S^2\, \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}\right) dt \;+\; \sigma S \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial S} - \Delta_t\right) dW_t

The same factor \big(\partial V/\partial S - \Delta_t\big) now multiplies both the \mu-dependent drift and the entire dW_t exposure.
Step 5 — substitute the hedge:
Substituting \Delta_t = \partial V/\partial S (the position q_t = -\Delta_t chosen above), both parentheses vanish at once,

d\Pi_t \;=\; \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \sigma^2 S^2\, \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}\right) dt
\tag{25}
Vanishing of the first parentheses means that the expected return of the stock (\mu) has disappeared from the hedged portfolio’s dynamics, meaning the option’s fair value doesn’t depend on it. This implies that two investors who disagree about the stock’s expected return still agree on the option’s price (provided they agree on the volatility \sigma and the risk-free rate r).
Similarly, vanishing of the second parentheses means that d\Pi_t has become independent of dW_t randomness entirely. So the same position choice q_t = -\Delta_t creates a portfolio that is delta-neutral and dW_t-free.
This is the crux of the construction. If we compare this with what we had before in Equation 22,

dV = \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} + \mu S \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2}\right) dt + \sigma S \frac{\partial V}{\partial S}\, dW_t

we find that a position whose return depended on the random fluctuations of S_t due to the presence of the dW_t term is rendered instantaneously risk-free, as we hedged away the dW_t exposure by adding stock to our portfolio.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
3.7 The Black-Scholes Equation
Because the hedged portfolio \Pi_t has no random component over [t, t+dt], we invoke the no-arbitrage condition and assert that it must earn the risk-free rate r — otherwise there would be a risk-free arbitrage. Thus:

d\Pi_t \;=\; r\, \Pi_t\, dt
\tag{26}
Substituting the portfolio definition \Pi_t = V(S_t, t) - \Delta_t\, S_t from Equation 24,

d\Pi_t \;=\; r\, \big[\, V(S_t, t) - \Delta_t\, S_t \,\big]\, dt

Using \Delta_t = \partial V/\partial S,

d\Pi_t \;=\; r\, \left[\, V \;-\; S_t\, \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} \,\right] dt

Equating the drift above with the drift from Equation 25,

\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2} = r V - r S \frac{\partial V}{\partial S}

Rearranging gives,

\boxed{\,\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} + r S \frac{\partial V}{\partial S} + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial S^2} = r V\,}

which is Equation 19. \square
It is worth pausing on what we have arrived at. This is the Black-Scholes equation, published by Fischer Black and Myron Scholes in 1973 [11] and, in the same year, set on a more general footing by Robert Merton [12]. It was the first time anyone had shown that a derivative could be priced by replication — that the option’s risk could be hedged away entirely, leaving a fair value fixed by no-arbitrage alone, independent of any investor’s risk appetite or view on the stock’s expected return. Its impact was immediate and enduring: it gave traders a closed-form price and a hedge ratio they could act on, and the derivatives markets that grew on top of it now run to hundreds of trillions of dollars in notional value. In 1997 the work was recognised with the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, awarded to Scholes and Merton; Black, who had died in 1995, could not share it, as the prize is not awarded posthumously, though the committee named his role explicitly.
For our purposes the equation is a landmark of a different kind: its second-order term \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2\,\partial_S^2 V — the one that distinguishes it from a deterministic pricing equation — traces back to the single rule (dW)^2 = dt — the same rule we are about to carry into diffusion models.

3.7.1 Solution to the Black-Scholes Equation
With the boundary condition V(S, T) = \max(S - K, 0) (Equation 20) for a European call, this PDE has the famous closed-form solution

\boxed{V(S, t) = S\, N(d_1) - K e^{-r(T-t)} N(d_2)}
\tag{27}
where N(\cdot) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function (CDF) and

d_1 = \frac{\log(S/K) + (r + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)(T-t)}{\sigma\sqrt{T-t}}, \quad d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T-t}

Solving the PDE (via change of variables to the heat equation) is a textbook exercise [13]; a step-by-step sketch is in Appendix A.2. The derivation we care about is everything up to the PDE.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
3.8 What the derivation establishes
The derivation has a clear logical structure:

We started with an SDE for S_t (the stock price).
We considered a function of that SDE: V(S, t) (the option value).
Itô’s lemma yielded the SDE for V.
The dW term in dV was hedgeable — we could remove the random component with a \Delta-position in the stock.
The hedged portfolio’s drift must match the risk-free rate, yielding a PDE for V.

The Itô correction term — \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 \partial_S^2 V — survives the hedging and becomes the second-order term in the PDE. Geometrically, it is the contribution of the option value’s curvature in S — the second derivative \partial_S^2 V, known in finance as the option’s gamma — weighted by the variance rate \sigma^2 S^2.
This structural fact is central: the second-order term in the BS PDE comes directly from (dW)^2 = dt. The same pattern appears in Part 4.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
4.1 What is a generative model?
Under a probabilistic framework, an observed dataset D can be considered a finite set of samples from an underlying unknown data distribution p_0. The goal of a generative model is to approximate this distribution by learning from the dataset D, so that the learned model can be used for inference, e.g. sampling.

4.1.1 Learning








Figure 10: Learning: choose a family \mathcal{M}=\{p_\theta\} and fit it to the data distribution p_0 by minimizing an objective d(p_0, p_\theta).





To approximate the distribution parametrically, we need three elements: a model family \mathcal{M} = \{p_\theta\} parameterized by \theta, an objective d(\cdot), and an optimization procedure that minimizes d(\cdot) [14], [15]. Generative learning is then the task of finding the optimal parameters \theta under that procedure, so that the objective d(\cdot) between the true data distribution p_0 and the model distribution p_\theta is minimized.


4.1.2 Inference
Once trained, a generative model answers three inference queries [14], [15]:

Density estimation: given x, return its probability p_\theta(x).
Sampling: generate new data x_{\text{new}} \sim p_\theta.
Representation learning: extract meaningful features of x.

Not every model family supports all three efficiently; the trade-offs drive the diversity of generative approaches.

title: Itô’s Lemma: From Black-Scholes to Diffusion Models
text:
4.2 What are diffusion models?
Diffusion models are a class of latent-variable generative models [2] — models that generate data through unobserved intermediate variables, here the noised states x_1, \ldots, x_N. A diffusion model has two components: the forward process and the reverse process. The forward process progressively adds noise to the training data until nothing but noise remains. The reverse process learns to undo that noising. Sampling starts from noise and runs the learned reverse process, producing new data such as images that resemble the training data.
Two parallel approaches to diffusion models developed independently, differing primarily in the objective d(\cdot): evidence lower bound (ELBO) and score-matching. The variational track minimizes the negative ELBO on the data log-likelihood. It runs from the nonequilibrium-thermodynamics formulation [16] to DDPM [2], where the bound is reparameterized as noise prediction. The score-based track minimizes a score-matching objective. It runs from score matching [17] through denoising score matching [18] to the noise-conditional score network [19]. Song et al. merged the two into a single framework in 2021 [1]. Figure 11 places these landmarks on a common timeline.








Figure 11: The two research lineages behind diffusion models, in chronological order. Left: the variational track, from the nonequilibrium-thermodynamics formulation to DDPM. Right: the score-based track, from score matching to the noise-conditional score network. The 2021 score-SDE paper merges them, showing the Variance-Preserving and Variance-Exploding constructions to be one equation.





The table maps each component of the generative-modeling framework to two key diffusion papers.
